case.title: Zenith Bank Plc v Mr Obaro Odeghe

procedural_history.originating_proceedings: Complaint filed on 13th August 2014 by the claimant against the defendant claiming recovery of mortgage and personal loans, interest, and unamortised value of a generator.
procedural_history.procedural_posture: The court raised the issue of jurisdiction suo motu and directed counsel to file written addresses. Parties adopted their written submissions on 2nd November 2015.
previous_decisions: Judgment of the Lagos High Court in Suit No ID/1088/2009 delivered in favour of the defendant, declaring entitlement to severance benefits and striking out the claimant's counterclaim.
procedural_events: Claimant filed complaint and motion for summary judgment on 13th August 2014.
Defendant filed statement of defence and counterclaim.
Court raised jurisdiction issue suo motu.
Claimant filed written address on 24th February 2015.
Defendant filed written address on 13th April 2015.
Claimant filed reply on point of law on 9th June 2015.
Parties adopted written submissions on 2nd November 2015.

material_facts: The defendant was an employee of the claimant.
The defendant obtained mortgage loans on 31st December 2007 and 21st March 2007, and a personal loan on 29th November 2005, during his employment.
The defendant resigned from the claimant's employment on 15th January 2008.
The claimant installed a 27 KVA generator at the defendant's private residence.
The defendant instituted Suit No ID/1088/2009 at the Lagos High Court against the claimant for severance benefits.
The Lagos High Court declared the defendant entitled to severance benefits and struck out the claimant's counterclaim regarding loans and generator.

chronology.event: Defendant applied for employee personal loan.
Defendant took personal loan of N6,000,000.
Defendant took mortgage loan of N19,000,000.
Defendant took mortgage loan of N30,000,000.
Defendant filed Suit No ID/1088/2009 at Lagos High Court.
Claimant filed complaint at National Industrial Court.
Parties adopted written submissions on jurisdiction.
Court delivered ruling striking out suit and counterclaim for want of jurisdiction.

disputed_facts: Whether the loans are recoverable as debts.

issues_for_determination.issue: Whether this Honourable Court has the jurisdiction to entertain the claimant’s suit as constituted.
Whether this Honourable Court has the jurisdiction to entertain the defendant’s counter claim as constituted.

Considering the nature of the claimant’s claim, Sections 272 and 254C (1) of the 1999 Constitution (as amended) and the final judgement of the Lagos State High Court in Suit No ID/1088/2009, does the National Industrial Court have jurisdiction to determine the claimant’s claim?

Considering the provisions of Section 254C (1) (k) of the 1999 Constitution (as amended), Order 18 Rule 1, of the National Industrial Court Rules, 2007, and the declaratory order of the High Court of Lagos State in Suit No ID/1088/2009 affirming the defendant’s right to his severance entitlement, does the National Industrial Court have the jurisdiction to determine defendant/counter-claimant’s counter-claim?

questions_of_law: Whether the National Industrial Court has jurisdiction over claims relating to recovery of loans granted by an employer to an employee.
Whether the counterclaim is barred by the doctrine of res judicata.
Whether the claims are statute barred under the Limitation Law of Lagos State.

claimant_arguments: The subject matter of the claim is the right of the employer to be repaid loans given to the defendant, which amounts to a debt.
The claim falls within Section 254C (1) (a) of the 1999 Constitution as amended.
The action is not statute barred because the defendant acknowledged the debt during cross-examination on 9th June 2010, within six years.
The court does not have jurisdiction to entertain the defendant’s counterclaim or to interpret the judgment of the Lagos State High Court.
The counterclaim is caught by the doctrine of res judicata.
The counterclaim is statute barred under Section 8 (1) of the Limitation Law of Lagos State.
defendant_arguments: The claimant’s claim has been determined in the final judgment of the Lagos High Court in Suit No ID/1088/2009, and no appeal was filed.
The National Industrial Court cannot sit on appeal over the decision of a State High Court.
The action is an abuse of the judicial process.
The claim is for recovery of mortgage sum and accrued interest arising from a simple mortgage contract, which is a banker/customer relationship, not an employment matter.
The counterclaim is a labour dispute arising from non-payment of severance benefits, which falls within Section 254C (1) of the 1999 Constitution.
The declaratory judgment of the High Court affirmed the right to 100% severance benefit, and the counterclaim seeks to ascertain the specific amount due.

party_authorities.authority: Thadani v National Bank of Nigeria Ltd [1972] 1 SC 75 at 80
party_authorities.proposition: Where a person liable has acknowledged the debt, the right of action is deemed to have accrued on the date of acknowledgement.
Court lacks jurisdiction to interpret judgment of co-ordinate court.

findings_of_fact.finding: The claims are in respect of mortgage and personal loans granted to the defendant during employment, and the alleged indebtedness.
The counterclaim relates to severance benefits already determined by the Lagos High Court in Suit No ID/1088/2009.

findings_of_law.finding: The National Industrial Court lacks jurisdiction over claims relating to loans and commercial transactions, as they do not fall within Section 254C (1) (a) & (k) of the 1999 Constitution.
The counterclaim is barred by the doctrine of res judicata as the issue of severance pay was finally determined by the Lagos High Court.

judicial_analysis.reasoning: The court held that jurisdiction is determined by the claimant's claim. The claims relate to recovery of loans, which are commercial transactions not connected to employment matters under Section 254C (1) (a) & (k). The counterclaim is res judicata because the Lagos High Court had already decided on severance benefits. Therefore, the court declined jurisdiction over both the suit and counterclaim.

issue_analysis.issue: Whether the National Industrial Court has jurisdiction to entertain the claimant’s suit.

arguments.claimant: The claim is for recovery of loans, which is a debt and falls within Section 254C (1) (a) of the Constitution.
arguments.defendant: The claim is a banker/customer relationship matter, not an employment matter, and the High Court has jurisdiction.

issue_analysis.judicial_analysis: The court examined the claims and found they relate to loans and commercial transactions, not employment matters. Section 254C (1) (a) & (k) does not cover such claims.
issue_analysis.holding: The court lacks jurisdiction to entertain the claimant’s suit.
issue_analysis.ratio_decidendi: The National Industrial Court's jurisdiction is limited to labour and employment matters; claims for recovery of loans, even if granted during employment, are commercial transactions outside its jurisdiction.
issue_analysis.result: Suit struck out for want of jurisdiction.

issue_analysis.issue: Whether the National Industrial Court has jurisdiction to entertain the defendant’s counterclaim.

arguments.claimant: The counterclaim is res judicata and statute barred.
arguments.defendant: The counterclaim is a labour dispute arising from non-payment of severance benefits, which falls within Section 254C (1) (k).

issue_analysis.judicial_analysis: The court found that the issue of severance benefits was already finally determined by the Lagos High Court in Suit No ID/1088/2009. The counterclaim is an attempt to re-litigate the same issue.
issue_analysis.holding: The counterclaim is barred by res judicata and the court lacks jurisdiction.
issue_analysis.ratio_decidendi: A counterclaim that seeks to re-litigate an issue already finally determined by a court of competent jurisdiction is barred by res judicata, and the National Industrial Court lacks jurisdiction to entertain it.
issue_analysis.result: Counterclaim struck out for want of jurisdiction.

holdings.holding: The court has no jurisdiction over the suit as it relates to loan recovery, not employment matters.
The counterclaim is res judicata and the court has no jurisdiction.

ratio_decidendi.application: The claimant's claims for loan recovery were outside the court's jurisdiction.

ratio_decidendi.principle: A counterclaim that re-litigates an issue already decided by a court of competent jurisdiction is barred by res judicata.
ratio_decidendi.application: The counterclaim for severance benefits was already determined by the Lagos High Court.

statutory_interpretation.interpretation: The provisions confer jurisdiction on the National Industrial Court for labour, employment, and related matters, but not for commercial transactions like loan recovery.

statutory_interpretation.interpretation: Actions founded on simple contract shall not be brought after six years from accrual of cause of action.

constitutional_analysis.interpretation: The jurisdiction of the National Industrial Court is limited to labour and employment matters, including payment or non-payment of salaries, wages, pensions, gratuities, allowances, benefits, and other entitlements.
constitutional_analysis.application: The court held that loan recovery claims are not within this jurisdiction.
